title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
summary: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.

title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.

title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
summary: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.

title: H3-Image Day-0 Support: 4K in 0.87s with Vera Rubin
summary: H3-Image on Vera Rubin: 0.87-second 4K generation or 6,115 images/hour on four GPUs, with projected API revenue and support across consumer and data-center hardware.
story_key: story|variant:image|title:h3 image day 0 support 4k in 0 87s with vera rubin
content_excerpt: We brought MiniMax H3-Image to NVIDIA Vera Rubin with vLLM-Omni. On four GPUs, native 4096×4096 generation reaches 0.87 seconds median in our short-prompt serving benchmark. A separate throughput configuration delivers 6,115 images/hour , projecting to 146,755 images/day . At USD 0.06879 per image , using MiniMax's official Standard 4K API pricing example before launch discounts as an assumed sale price, peak throughput projects to USD 105.16/GPU/hour in gross revenue at full billable utilization, or USD 78.87/GPU/hour at 75%. These estimates are before operating costs; the daily capacity is an extrapolation of the measured rate. H3-Image is an open-weight model for text-to-image generation and image editing. One checkpoint handles both tasks in six sampling steps, generates native high-resolution images without an upscaler, and supports up to 16 reference images. We bring H3-Image to consumer and data-center GPUs , spanning NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Moore Threads (MUSA) , as well as Huawei Ascend NPUs . Oil-paint strokes, a multi-view camera drawing, Japanese poster lettering and tiny words on a rice grain reveal what a smaller image can lose. A game environment adds weathered stone and reflected light. Each uses one H3-Image-generated 4K image, resized to 1K and 2K with its aspect ratio preserved, so composition stays fixed. The two API modes are straightforward: Text-to-Image takes a prompt; Image Edit takes a prompt and one or more reference images. Our main comparisons use 2K (2048×2048) and 4K (4096×4096) output, with one image returned per request. The prompts and reference files stay fixed across machines. See MiniMax's API guide for the request parameters. Choose Text-to-image or Image Edit below. For editing, select 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 reference images ; output sizes reflect the measured cases. For 4K text-to-image , four GB300 GPUs average 1.48 seconds . A 4K image edit with one reference averages 1.77 seconds . A single RTX 5090 with CPU layerwise offload takes 52.29 seconds and 61.45 seconds for those same requests. Each timing includes the complete PNG response. For 2K text-to-image , a single H200 averages 1.49 seconds with BF16 and resident weights. For the detailed coffee-product prompt used here, Rubin averages 1.09 seconds at 4K. The 0.87-second headline comes from a separate short-prompt serving benchmark in Rubin Bringup , not this request. Both use four GPUs, SP4 and MXFP8; the request corpus, HTTP client and summary statistic differ. Every

title: New AI agent observability and governance across BigQuery and Looker
summary:
As enterprises move AI agents from experimental prototypes into production, data and platform teams are discovering that deploying an agent is only half the battle — you also need to see how it reasons, which data it touches, and what it costs to run. Today, we are announcing expanded AI agent observability and evaluation capabilities across Google Data Cloud, giving you unified visibility into your first-party (1P) data agents in BigQuery and Looker as well as custom third-party (3P) agents built with agent development frameworks such as Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph.

Putting conversational and autonomous agents into production requires solving three operational challenges: tracing multi-step reasoning while protecting sensitive data, controlling token consumption and query spend, and evaluating answer accuracy before prompt or schema changes reach users. Let’s explore how our new agent observability and evaluation capabilities help you do this. 

What's new: Agent observability across Data Cloud

Running agents at scale means you need to see how they perform, what they cost, and what actions they take. We're rolling out a unified telemetry framework across Google's Agentic Data Cloud that works the same way for every agent: Capture telemetry from the agent, land it in BigQuery tables you own, and analyze it wherever your teams already work.

1. Capture telemetry from every first-party and custom agent

  • First-party data agents: Out-of-the-box Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically with no setup required. Queries routed to BigQuery data agents in Gemini Enterprise through agent-to-agent (A2A) workflows (now GA) send Cloud Monitoring metrics, Cloud Trace spans, and BigQuery conversation logs straight into your agent's project.

  • Custom agents: Agents built with ADK or LangGraph stream the same structured telemetry into BigQuery through single-line SDK instrumentation.

2. Land telemetry in one governed home in BigQuery

  • Conversation logging in BigQuery (GA): Managed 1P conversation logging writes to BigQuery tables you own, so you can inspect Conversational Analytics traces, including prompts and responses, directly in your data warehouse.

  • Governed by default: The Conversational Analytics API, now GA, includes always-on admin audit logs and optional data-read audit logs in Cloud Audit Logs, and supports VPC Service Controls, customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and regional and multi-regional data residency.

3. Analyze with dashboards wherever your teams work

  • In BigQuery (GA): Agent monitoring provides prebuilt dashboards in BigQuery Studio to track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency across BigQuery Conversational Analytics agents.

  • In Looker (GA): System Activity dashboards for Conversational Analytics, now GA in Looker (Google Cloud core) and Looker (original), track engagement and token usage, while user ratings and query review in the Responses & feedback tab are in preview.
  • Build your own: Create interactive reports with the open-source Data Studio template or deploy the ready-made Looker Block for Agent Analytics for real-time custom agent monitoring.

Tracing agent reasoning and protecting privacy

Enterprise observability requires balancing diagnostic telemetry with strict data privacy boundaries. Because tracking features involve ingestion and storage costs, Google Data Cloud separates operational telemetry from conversation content so admins and agent owners can govern each layer independently.

At the project or organization level, admins can enable Cloud Monitoring (aggregate metrics such as request volume, latency, and token usage) and Cloud Trace (step-by-step spans for each request) across their environment, using Cloud Trace observability scopes to consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects. To protect sensitive data, these operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content (such as user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts, and generated SQL).

When you need deeper transcript auditing, agent owners and editors can opt in to conversation logging on a per-agent basis:

  • Governed conversation logging in BigQuery: When enabled, a Google-managed service agent streams user prompts, responses, and turn-level telemetry into a customer-owned BigQuery table (agent_events) via the BigQuery Storage Write API, inheriting your dataset's IAM permissions, CMEK, and VPC Service Controls. Built-in privacy guardrails enforce a fail-closed check before each turn — skipping logging whenever a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags, or dynamic data masking — while fail-open execution keeps your users' chat sessions uninterrupted if a logging error occurs.

  • Full trace trees for custom 3P agents: While 1P conversation logging intentionally strips low-level tool arguments and internal SQL, developers building custom agents on ADK or LangGraph can instrument their code with the open-source ADK plugin (BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin). With a single-line setup, the SDK streams full tool-invocation execution trees, time-series telemetry, and multimodal payloads straight into BigQuery.

  • In-warehouse root cause and drift analysis: Because conversation logs land natively in your agent_events table, you don't need separate export pipelines to diagnose failures. You can run BigQuery AI functions (such as AI.GENERATE to summarize error patterns and AI.EMBED with VECTOR_SEARCH to cluster recurring issues) or use the open-source bigquery-agent-analytics Python SDK and Colab starter notebook for post-hoc semantic drift clustering and LLM-as-a-judge sentiment analysis.

Controlling token costs with FinOps guardrails

As agent adoption grows, FinOps and platform teams need clear visibility into consumption alongside active controls to prevent runaway spend. With promotional trial pricing currently available for Conversational Analytics, now is a good time to establish baseline usage and cost guardrails:

  • Granular token and latency tracking: In BigQuery conversation logs, each turn records input, output, thought, cached, and total token counts alongside total turn latency, while Looker System Activity reports estimated input and output tokens across your business intelligence (BI) workloads.

  • Turnkey observability dashboards: You can track projected token usage and engagement in the BigQuery Studio Monitoring tab and native Looker System Activity dashboards, or query agent_events log data via BigQuery SQL using the open-source seven-page Data Studio report template and self-hosted Streamlit app in the BigQuery Agent Analytics GitHub repository.

  • Active query and token spend caps: To prevent unexpected charges before they happen, you can configure per-query BigQuery byte scan caps (big_query_max_billed_bytes) on your agent, which use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. For BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API, you can also enforce daily input and output token quotas (in preview) per project, user, or agent in the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI.

Evaluating and benchmarking your AI agents

Runtime observability works alongside systematic evaluation. While logs and traces tell you how an agent behaved in production, evaluation benchmarks verify whether updates to your prompts, models, or data schemas improve SQL accuracy and answer quality before users experience a regression:

  • Benchmarking with Prism: Our open-source evaluation tool, Prism, lets you test Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores via the Conversational Analytics API using reusable test suites, regex assertions, and multi-region agent discovery (deployed behind an access layer such as Cloud IAP).

  • Unified evaluation and production analytics: Prism can stream completed evaluation runs directly into day-partitioned BigQuery tables in your project, placing your pre-deployment benchmark scores right alongside your production agent_events logs for side-by-side analysis in BigQuery and Looker.

  • Native BigQuery evaluations: First-party agent evaluations in BigQuery (built on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform evaluation service with bring-your-own-service-account support) are available in preview via API and a guided Colab notebook.

Getting started

Ready to bring visibility, governance, and cost control to your AI agents? Here is how to get started in three steps:

  1. Enable first-party agent observability. Turn on Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace in your project and opt in to per-agent conversation logging using the BigQuery agent monitoring guide, and track BI token consumption with the Looker Conversational Analytics overview and Looker System Activity documentation.

  2. Instrument custom agents and deploy analytics dashboards. Add the BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK to your ADK or LangGraph agents, launch the open-source Data Studio report template or Streamlit app, and explore in-warehouse log analysis with the Colab starter notebook.

  3. Benchmark your agents and set cost guardrails. Run automated accuracy suites with Prism, and configure BigQuery byte scan caps and daily token quotas via Manage BigQuery costs for agents.

title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
summary: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.

title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
summary: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.
